utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before resuming the cross-examination of Mr. Fraser, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you indicated yesterday you would leave a bit earlier. Would that be after the second break or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I guess it will be around noon and I will take the liberty to leave, unfortunately not waiting for the break, but around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking you because the Stakic case is not sitting this afternoon, so that would mean that we would have some extra time if this could be scheduled. If we would split up the day in two parts, we would gain a bit more than half an hour. On the other hand, I am aware -- I do take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you accepted more or less that, well, the last one hour and-a-half would be in your absence. May I first ask you whether you would heavily oppose, if that would be instead of one hour and-a-half, two hours. I take it you are so organised --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you are asking me personally, I must say that personally, of course, I have resistance to this solution. However, this does not apply to Mrs. Pilipovic, who was sick this week and who nevertheless attended. And in my absence, she wouldn't be able to really check the transcript and at the same time to continue exercising the efforts which she is investing here and which is most harrowing. So I am afraid, as I have said, because it is not my personal response, my answer cannot be positive. As for Mr. Galic, who is sitting behind me, he told me when we could visit him in this regard that he can never sufficiently concentrate when days drag on much longer into the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about half an hour, not more than three-quarters of an hour. Put, please, if you would express yourself on it, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the past six months were really hard work for the Defence and I was not feeling well this week, but if it is not more than half an hour, then I will ask the General what he thinks. I should also like to remind you that our military expert is here in The Hague and we would like to know when Mr. Philipps's examination will begin so our military expert can come and be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we have in the order of half an hour or forty minutes to go with Mr. Fraser, something like that. I anticipate that Mr. Bergeron in chief will be something like an hour at the most. Therefore, I expect that we will reach the evidence of Mr. Philipps today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And, of course, in a timetable, he is designated to reappear after General Van Baal on Monday. I have only, at the most, five minutes with General Van Baal, so I expect to have one hour or two hours of the testimony of Mr. Philipps again on Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. How about the Prosecution? I think final arrangements will either be made or not made during the first break, but I am just trying to make an inventory of what the parties could --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am very much in favour of it. We are falling behind this week considerably and that would help to minimise that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. So at least I now know the positions of the parties, not yet of the accused. Did you confer with General Galic, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Galic believes, considering the state of his health, that he told us before the beginning of trial already that he has contracted a virus and has been under the weather for the past week. So the question is whether he can keep his concentration and follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so I do understand that there is considerable hesitation on his side. On the other hand, we also might consider to see how things go and ask General Galic to intervene when there would be a situation where he loses concentration to such extent that he would think it fair to stop at that time. But we will consider that during the first break and see whether the schedule changes or not. Then, Ms. Pilipovic, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Fraser? Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not Mrs. Pilipovic who will do it. It will be myself, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Mrs. Pilipovic will take over for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fraser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that your are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To save time, we shall do it like this. I will submit to you a list of names, and if these names or a name ring a bell with you, then you will stop me and you tell me about it. Can we agree about that? I have to tell that all these names, of course, have to do with Sarajevo: Kobra, Sultan Fatih, Kulin Ban, Stela, Borsalino, Silos, Gras, Pavle Goranin, Petar Dakic. These names don't tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Caco?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ljiljana?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fikret?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of Fikrets, but you would have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Because in your statement, Witness, you mentioned that you had met several times a certain person called Fikret. Who is the Fikret whom you used to meet?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Fikret who commanded the brigade just on the other side of the airport that we used to visit and it was in the Butmir area, and he also had the Igman Mount, but I don't know what his real name was. That was the name that we heard him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since you visited him, could you tell us where was his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the Butmir area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And more exactly?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be any more specific than that. It was just in that general area just before you hit the mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the BH army under his control?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I had to check the transcript. Yes. My question was: Did he control the BH army? Did he control the BH army, not whether the BH army was under his control. And that is not the same thing. My question was: [In English] Was he under the control of the BH army? That was the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Colonel, I go back to the elements which I gave you, which are only partial, but now I would like to ask you the following question. You spoke about attacks on civilians. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in your statement and in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, did you speak about attacks on civilians who were going to fetch water, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall talking about attacks on people getting water, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know where were armament factories, and by this I mean factories of whatever size?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was lots of discussion about armaments factories. I did not personally know where the actual locations of these factories were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Do you know that there were some factories in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We knew there were factories, but I did not know where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Do you know whether there was a foundry, also?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say a foundry, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am speaking about a shop which specialises in foundring and recasting the explosives which is -- treats the explosives so that they could be reused again in other weapons.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there was discussion that there were places like that, but I have no personal knowledge of where those places were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel, do you know - I believe you said so but I do not know - were there mobile targets such as trucks, lorries, transformed, that is the ones which could be used for mortars, for mortars to fire from the?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that, from time to time, the BiH army would fire from the city and the British and the French would try to find these firing units, but were never successful because they were never where we could locate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question had to do specifically with mobile targets.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is it possible to make a break between the answer and the question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure I quite understand when you say "mobile targets."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "mobile targets," Colonel, I mean -- by "mobile targets," I mean a truck which has a mounted mortar on it, for instance.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we did when we would hear outgoing firing we knew were mortars, we would go out and try to find them, but we never did find them because we just were -- you know, when we went to the area where the sound came from, there was nothing there. So I never saw, or the people who went looking never saw the firing unit. Whether it was on the ground or on a vehicle, we didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I have to interrupt you. Did you ever hear speaking while you were there about such mobile targets; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, did you, yourself, personally know of the following incidents of the 27th May, 1994; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date doesn't ring anything -- bring anything to mind, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I repeat for the transcript, the 25th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am not sure whether that is fair, just to put the date to the witness without specifying the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will add the names. I will be very happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 25th of May, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Plivac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 13th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. President. Just a little specificity about what kind of incident is it, is it an incident involving some type of injury or weaponry or a location --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I think it is up to the Defence to put questions to the witness, and if they would limit and say: "Do you know anything about an attack on the 3rd of January," then of course there is a fair chance that if the date or just one simple name doesn't mention anything to the witness, where the witness might have some recollection if he was better informed then, of course, the answer you get on these kind of questions will be assessed in such a way, of course, in view of the question. So if I say "25th of October" and the witness says, "No," then of course the Chamber is aware that there is a fair chance that the witness does not know because he has not been provided with sufficient information. And I am certain that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is aware that this is, I would say, more or less a logical consequence of the way he puts his questions. I don't know whether he seeks an answer of a witness that he doesn't know about a certain incident or that he does know. I do not know. But the questions are such we will leave that to the Defence, and the Defence will be fully aware that the way they put the question to the witness is sometimes very indicative for the answer you might expect. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President. I will be more specific, more than the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are certainly aware that if one witness has a very good recollection, for example, for dates, that does not automatically mean that if another witness would not respond immediately to dates, that the Chamber would automatically accept that the witness is fully informed about the incident he is asked about. So I leave it up to you, but you are aware of the consequences of the way you put questions to the witness, I take it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The incident of the 25th of May, 1994, was on Nikole Demonje Street, not far from Bulevar Avnoja. It doesn't tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The incident of the 13th of June, 1994, which involved a woman, Sulcin [phoen], of about 44 years of age at the time in the Ive Andrica Street. It rings no bell, either?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The incident of the 19th of June, 1994, one Jasmin Kucinar, who was 31, and his son Damir Kucinar, who was about 4, and who were attacked in relation to an incident to an attack on a tram. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were numerous attacks on the tram, but that doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same day, Mensur Jusic, 36; Belma Sukic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. 26th June, 1994, attack involving a person of 16, Sanela Muratovic, in Djure Jaksica Street?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The 17th of June, 1994, Mr. Rashid Dzonko, 67 at that time, who was -- who was a conductor, who drove or operated an industrial machine, does he mean anything to you? Milanko Vitomir Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think if the incident of the 17th of June as it was put to the witness, it probably meant July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, yes, July. July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: July, but same question.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same on the 22 of July, 1994, involving certain [redacted], who was wounded not far from Cengic Vila?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please redact? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel does not have his microphone switched on. Your microphone is still not switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you could have asked for closed session, if necessary. So therefore -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your answer "no" again?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you know of a statement given by Mr. Wahlgren, who was a General who was also posted in Sarajevo, and who said that -- he said that there were many military targets in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the General in question you are talking about. Were there military targets in Sarajevo? Along the confrontation line, you could say the military headquarters were a military target, but you would have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Colonel. You said earlier -- or not earlier but rather yesterday, asked by the Prosecution, you answered that in fact in Sarajevo there were only civilians and there were no military. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was in specific areas, yes, there were civilians and the UN. There were -- the BiH army were along the confrontation line, they had their headquarters. But were there other military targets? I mean, it is a big city. You will have to be a little bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I will be specific if I tell you that each of the names that I listed for you earlier, Petar Dakic, Pavle Goranin and so on, they are in fact locations of military targets. Would you agree with me to say that you did not know anything of the locations of the military targets?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with you because I just don't know the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. specifics. I mean, there was a war going on and we saw shooting and firing on both sides. Sometimes it was towards another person in the other side's army, but in a lot of cases it was directed towards civilians who had no military value.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel, since you do not agree with me, could you please tell me where is the headquarters of Kobra?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the headquarters of Kobra is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Where is the headquarters of the Ljiljana group?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Where is the headquarters of Kulin Ban, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And so on, do you think you could tell us the headquarters of other locations that I quoted to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't because I didn't deal with those headquarters. I dealt with the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Therefore, you do not know where these military targets are in the city, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have personal knowledge. You would have to ask people who would have that knowledge. I dealt with the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer means that you do not -- did not have that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I did not know where those locations were, if they existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Colonel, do you know accurately - and I would be grateful if you could answer with a yes or no - where was the headquarters of the command of the following brigades: 101st, 102nd, the 1st, the 2nd, the 1st Motorised Brigade, the 2nd Motorised Brigade, the 5th Motorised Brigade, the 9th Motorised Brigade and the 10th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you that information now it's been so long. And, again, I dealt with the corps headquarters, with the government agencies --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to have to interrupt you, Colonel, for -- in order not to waste time. I believe that you will answer the same for the command posts on the level of battalions that are more numerous than those of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battalions were dealt with by the regiments within the sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, my question was not that. My question was that I believe that your answer would be the same for the level of the battalions.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Colonel, how could you state that such-and-such rounds or firing that you were able to observe were of an indiscriminate character if you do not know even where in Sarajevo such-and-such targets were located, such-and-such military targets were located?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because normally, a professional army would not engage another person's headquarters if it was co-located in a civilian community. Like what I explained yesterday, why we knew there was a tank in the Serbian area but because of collateral damage and the potential of killing or injuring civilians, we wouldn't go after them. But the Serbians didn't take that into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Colonel, is that it was perfectly possible that there were military targets but the Serbs should not have attacked them because they were located in the city?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am saying is that every attack that happened was, for the most part, was investigated by us and we would protest it based on the merits of that attack

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was not my question, Colonel. You are not answering my question, Colonel. My question, I would be grateful if you could re-read it but I am going to repeat it. What you are saying is that it may have happened that there were military targets in the city but that the Serbs should not have attacked them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said was that where there are military targets along the confrontation line and the other side engaged it, we looked at that and observed it but we did not comment because that was a legal military engagement. Where targets were engaged in the city, we would investigate, and where there were civilians involved, you were certain we were going to protest it because that was not a military target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is still not the answer to my question. If we assume that there were legitimate military targets in the city, the Serb army, could it have attacked them; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my experience, during the time we are talking about, for example, like the Bosnian Corps headquarters was never attacked when I was there, nor was the Serbian Corps headquarters in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not an answer to the question. The question was not whether other military targets were ever attacked. But the question was quite clear, I think, and that is that if there would have been military targets within the city, whether the Serbs would have had to refrain from attacking it because of the collateral damage, as you explained it yesterday. Yesterday, you said: "We would not go after the tank because of the collateral damage." The question now is: If there were headquarters or if there were military targets in the city, whether the Serbian forces would have had to refrain from attacking it because of the collateral damage it could cause. That is the question, I think, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did not even add about collateral damage because sometimes collateral damage comes naturally. But, in general, that was the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there was a military target in the city, the Serbs had a right to go after the military target and the UN would not protest that because that was within the rules of engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. President, I would like the map to be submitted again to the Colonel that was submitted yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in such a way so that we can see the eastern part of Sarajevo, please, the most interesting part for the questions, please, for the exercise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you see this map before you. General, could you please indicate on this map where are located the headquarters of the MUP, M-u-p. General?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Colonel. I apologise. There are so many stripes that I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is okay. I can't tell you where the MUP headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't tell me because you don't know or because it is a bad map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, did you wish to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is what I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Colonel. So I take note that you cannot answer the question. Could you please indicate on this map where was the 10th Mountain Brigade located?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Fikret again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. No, Fikret was not 10th Mountain Brigade, it was something else.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Wasn't it well put?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a question whether or not it was well put. It is just my knowledge of the brigades, I just don't have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not know where the 10th Brigade is, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please indicate the area where Fikret was, the Fikret's Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the Butmir area, that is about as specific as I can be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Colonel, you said that the sniper units of the other side were using, in order to fire, they were using the Unis tower and also the building that was known as the legislative building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please indicate that on the map, Colonel, where that is located. And if you can, could you please mark it with a pen of a different colour. It should be black, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was near the Holiday Inn. I just can't tell from this map the two towers. I can give you a general area, if that is all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You can perhaps put just a cross so that we do not make a confusion. On the area of Unis, if you can put a letter "U" next to it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it has been some time so I can't tell --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, if you can't, Colonel, we will take note. Colonel, can you please indicate on this map where is the area of Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that case, where are going to ask other questions. Do you know if there were incidents, as far as you know, incidents against Serb citizens on the 1st of May that you may know about, or on the 3rd of May in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if on the 14th of May, there were also incidents, sniping incidents, that as a result killed civilians, injured four, very near the brigade called Ilijas Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On the -- I will just check the dates. On the 15th of May, also, the very same question in relation to a man called Zoran Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the 21st of May, do you know if there were incidents where civilians were wounded in relation to Vogosca and Blagovac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. 30th of May in Grbavica, there was a child who was injured?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, do you know in which rhythm where combat went on between the warring arms?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're -- your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the rhythm of fighting, of battles, of combats, the frequency of fighting between the two warring armies?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the period of time that we are talking about, it became more intense, particularly sniping and shelling. And whenever the BiH would attack, the Serbs would retaliate disproportionately in most cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On the map, could you show us, General, where did the shellings take place that you knew about? If you can also tell us when, if you can precisely tell us the dates.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you general areas. I cannot give you specific dates because that information is not at the tip of my tongue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please take the pointer and indicate the exact area.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can tell you re: areas but not specific areas, specific points. Jewish cemetery was an area, and again from this map, it is somewhat difficult. It has been some time. There was something going on up in this area here and out at, from time to time, at the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel, could you please take a black pen and circle this little area, but please make a square rather than a circle so that we do not have a visual confusion.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the airport area, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, it is in these areas that the shellings occurred?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Colonel, I am going to come back to one of the things that you said yesterday. You said that near the sniper alley, there were only civilians. That is what you said. Colonel, how can you tell apart a soldier from a civilian?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think there were very many soldiers who were under the age of 10. And so when we heard there were children being shot, we pretty well ruled out that those were soldiers. When we heard that people were being shot on trams, we ruled out that they were soldiers. But again, when there was a shooting, if it was against a soldier, that was considered a military target, but when it was against what we would -- could prove were noncombatants, that's when a protest to be lodged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel, you didn't quite answer my question. In Sarajevo, how could you -- how would you tell apart a soldier from a civilian, if we agree that a young child of 4, 5 or 10 years old is not a soldier? What would be the difference between a soldier and a civilian?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were armed and wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Therefore, if there was a body that you saw, hypothetically, which was not in uniform and had no more weapons or no weapons, then you would say that was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a body, no weapon, no uniform, and the investigation said that that was the case, then we would probably, in that hypothetical case, we would probably say that was not a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the investigation, who was in charge of that? Local authorities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of people that would conduct investigations, UNMOs, the unit in the area where the incident took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please give me a list, if you can recall, of examples of incidents involving -- in sniping incidents, investigation done by UNMOs where you had also taken part?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take personally part in the investigations. I would be receiving the reports from the units or the UNMOs coming up to the sector headquarters, and I can't give you any details because there were numerous ones. It was just my general recollection of the incidents over that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to give us at least one example, a specific example, that you would have remembered where there was an investigation which was carried out, say, by UNPROFOR and that you knew about during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can give you what sticks in my mind. There were some incidents. I can't give you the specific dates, but I can indicate to you there was one shooting in the city on the tram, where some people were shot and killed and they were identified as civilians. There was another incident where there was a bus going outside of the city, going to another community, and along the route, a mother was shot on the bus. And I know that one in particular because General Soubirou went out and actually did the -- he was there on the scene shortly after the incident took place. So those two stick out in mind. But I would have to refer to my own notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel, two questions: When you say, "going to another community," you are using this expression in order to designate a different ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a bus that went from Sarajevo and I believe it went up north, out of the city, to -- I can't remember the name of the town. But again, the details are somewhat cloudy. But in that one particular case, there was a shooting and a woman was shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And every time there were written reports that were compiled and were kept by UNPROFOR authorities?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every case, there was a report and it was logged in either the unit or the sector situation reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this also went for the shellings and the snipings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as possible. Sometimes the soldiers were overwhelmed by the volume of shelling. They would try to count the number of impacts per day, but it was an art, not a science.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom were these reports addressed? And this is one of my very last questions. Who was then responsible? To whom were these reports addressed, if you know that? No. To whom were these reports addressed on the side -- on the side of the allegedly responsible side, if that was ever sent there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two reports would be generated out of an incident: The report to the sector headquarters that something happened and what were the details. Based on the report, then we would protest, if a protest was warranted, to the applicable corps headquarters indicating to them the incident. And as I said yesterday, for the most part, we would try to follow up that with a personal meeting with the respectable -- respective Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. headquarters, to try to defuse the situation and resolve those incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be the last question of the Defence or just a few, because I notice that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is the very last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but of you as the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The very last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I just like to come back to one of the things that you said in your statement. If we have soldiers who do not wear a uniform and who are sharing a weapon, are they still, in your opinion, logical military targets that are acceptable?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone picks up a weapon, then they become a military target if they use that weapon in an offensive manner towards the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, your answer means that if two soldiers are operating, are deployed, and they are sharing one weapon, they then constitute a military target?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person with the weapon would be a military target. The other person, if they are not dressed like a soldier, in my estimation, are not a military target if I can't identify them as doing something belligerent to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Waespi, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Re-examined by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, following up on the last question of the Defence, at that time, did all the soldiers from the BiH army wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them did, not all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, and I would like to ask you for a clarification, you answered to a question by the Defence, and I quote you - it was about sniping from the Presidency side - the quote is: "In the incident where there was sniping from the Muslim side, it would be against the Serbs, on their side of the confrontation line." By "on their side of the confrontation line," you mean which side, the Serb side, Serbs living on the Serb side, or Serbs living on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about on the Serbian side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Fraser. And the last clarification: You were asked this morning, and I quote the question from the Defence, about "the rhythm of fighting, of battles and combats, between the two warring factions." And your answer was, and I quote you: "Whenever the BH would attack, the Serbs would retaliate, disproportionately in most cases." Can you explain what you mean by, "disproportionately."

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if the BiH sniped against the Serb side, we could expect a lot more sniping coming back against the Muslim side from the Serbs disproportionately. The general discussion around UN soldiers was that it was almost -- it looked like something like a 10-to-1 type of scenario, and we could always expect something a lot more significant. If the Muslims had shelled the Serbian side with a few mortar rounds, we could expect a tremendous amount of shelling coming back against the Muslims. The Serbians were very good and it was just a matter of time when they retaliated, or what the French would say "riposte." It would be far more violent and significant than what was going out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you just answered relates only to military activity, military -- legitimate military action, also against civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the entire spectrum. It didn't matter whether it was military or civilian. The rhythm was about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have an additional question which was not raised in cross-examination, but I've asked the Defence whether I would be allowed. It is just a question to who his predecessor was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did the Defence agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, they did agree

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, my last question is: Who was your predecessor in your function?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My predecessor was a Major Christian Bergeron.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know whether there were military personnel in the Tito Barracks during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- the French were there, some Ukrainians were there, and for a while, there were some Bosnian soldiers in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that there were some BH snipers, units, somewhere. And do you know the positions of those snipers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BiH snipers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would move around. We knew where there were some buildings. We believed they fired out of the Unis building. And there were some buildings across the street and along sniper alley they would use. When we tried to press the corps, General Karavelic, about those positions or try to investigate where those positions were, we were always prevented or we couldn't find them. But we would actively go out and try to stop the BiH from doing these actions against -- based on if it was against nonmilitary targets on the other side. But we did the same thing on the Serb side. So we knew where the areas were, but snipers wouldn't go back to the same spot all the time because they wouldn't last very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well. You told us that you couldn't indicate on the map Grdonj.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember now where Grdonj is. It is near Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you testified about it yesterday and you were asked whether you could indicate it on the map. So you know the approximate location of Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I now remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked questions about attacking military objects that would be located in the city. It was not quite clear to me your answer in that respect. If you would be allowed to attack such a military object, although located in an area which was predominantly civilian, would there be any restrictions as to the means you would use to attack such an object, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view as a soldier, understanding the law of armed conflict, to attack a city, first of all, I personally wouldn't do it. But if someone was going to do it, I would not use indirect fire weapons at all because of the collateral damage and the footprint. You cannot reasonably expect that a mortar is going to land where you want it to land, or an artillery shell, without guided munitions. And at that time, neither side had them that I was aware of. In that case, I would only use a direct fire weapon that could minimise collateral damage and it would have to be against a very specific target. But again, firing into a city is fraught with danger, and in my opinion, I mean, the use of indirect fire was just -- there was very little way of getting to the target you were going after. There was just too much probability of error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would be the way to do it if you would like to attack - it is a hypothetical question, I am aware of that - what means you would deem to be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to a lot of observation on the position. I would want to make sure that there were no civilians or noncombatants in the area, to minimise collateral damage, and I would use the weapons system that gave me the highest probability to get that with minimizing all the potential possibilities of hitting something that I didn't want to get hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. You would like to have all the civilians removed and then to choose your weapon. But let' just assume in a densely populated area, you couldn't get rid of all the civilians around, well, the headquarters or storage of military material. What, after you very well observed the target, what would be your military weapons suitable for such an attack? Or would there be no --

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sniper would be the only thing I would use. A high-qualified sniper with a rifle with a high-powered scope on it. If I was going after something that I needed a lot of precision, that is about the best thing you could use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And let's just assume that the -- well, let's call it the military headquarters, was in a building when there was no direct sight from your positions to, well, let's say the lower storeys of that building, would that still make snipers a suitable weapon to attack that military object?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What alternative would you then have?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about something of a larger calibre weapon or something. Now you are getting outside and you are getting into collateral damage. It is a difficult -- it is a difficult problem to get through. How do you get inside to a target that is surrounded by noncombatants? It is a soldier's worst nightmare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, sir. Colonel Fraser, you have responded to -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not perhaps all the questions. Now it is 30 seconds, if that much, because one of the questions which we wanted to ask following your intervention was to do with your question. For the reasons that we know and in relation to this question of the Chamber, there is something which I would like the Colonel to tell us, if he knows. Thank you very much. Further cross-examination by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, do you know, yes or no, do you have any knowledge if -- whether the headquarters, the general headquarters, were, in a general manner, in a manner of speaking, on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about headquarters in general or which --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about the major part of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my recollection of going both to the BiH headquarters or the army headquarters or the corps headquarters, they were in buildings of two to three storeys, if I recall, and the General's office that we went and visited was always on the first level. You go upstairs and it was on the first level. Now -- but the headquarters had more than one floor and so, I mean, there were offices on all the floors. But the General's office that we went and visited was always on the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first floor?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first floor, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you do not know whether other headquarters were situated on ground floors or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to say that you answered all the questions but you did not yet. But now you have done so. You have answered all the questions both of the -- or am I wrong, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just one clarification again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On this very issue, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: About headquarters. Further re-examination by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, you said that the headquarters were not generally targeted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there a direct sight between the headquarters --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must object to this question. I do not think that that was the Colonel's testimony. He said that, generally speaking, the Presidency was not targeted, not the headquarters in plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to find the place. Could you indicate where it was, Mr. Waespi? Otherwise, I will try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The point, Mr. President, I am trying to make is the Defence asked in what storeys the headquarters were. And my question, and I don't need to refer to an earlier testimony, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you rephrase the question without referring to any earlier testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether there was any direct sight between the storeys where headquarters were to the areas where the weaponry of the warring factions were, in particular, the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question phrased as it is cannot be answered because we know that there is a considerable number of command posts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all of them or just about a few of them. We will hear from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Fraser, can you answer the question in a general way that there was a direct line of sight between the headquarters you had visited, had the chance to visit, and the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- General Galic's headquarters was in a more open area. It was not in as built-up an area as the BiH. And just outside the front gate there was, as I recall, some farm fields and whatnot. So it was in a barracks that was a little bit more easily accessible. So I mean -- was there a direct line of sight to that complex? I think there was more a line of sight to that complex than there was for the BiH, which was in the city, and it was in buildings that were downtown. So, depending where you were, you might see it, but it is in the middle of town so it is just a bunch of buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Fraser.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I again will tell you that you answered all the questions, I am looking around very carefully. You did, both the questions of the parties and the questions of the Bench. I thank you very much for having come and testify in this court. Thank you very much. And, Mr. Usher, can you please escort Colonel Fraser out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please escort us through the ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3644.DF, map marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I would like to spend a couple of minutes on another issue and ask some information from the parties. There is a motion of the 14th of July 2000 inviting -- no, I think we should first go into closed session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the sake of the record, we turned into open session a couple of minutes too late. We discussed practical issues and nothing else. Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the witness and that will be, Mr. Waespi, Mr. Bergeron?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, may I ask you to put your headphones on? I take it that you hear me in a language you understand but someone else in this courtroom might speak a different language and then you might not be in a position to follow what has been said. Mr. Bergeron, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration? And the text of that declaration will be handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may be seated. To start with, you will be examined by the counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bergeron. Can you please state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to apologise, I am apologising now, because I was stopped by the security guards, is that Mr. Galura wanted to know everything about me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, who would not like to know everything about you. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, can you please state for the record your name and your rank?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I am Lieutenant-Colonel Christian Bergeron. I am a member of Canadian Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to serve in the Balkans in a UN capacity?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. I served with the UNPROFOR from April 1993 until April 1994. I started with the three weeks at the UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb and then I was moved to the Sector Sarajevo until April 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your role when you served in Sarajevo between April, after these three weeks, 1993, and April 1994?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I worked directly for the commander of the Sarajevo Sector. I could summarise my position as I was a chef de cabinet of the commander of the Sarajevo Sector. My main duties was to accompany the commander of the sector wherever he went and to also attend all the meetings, whether it was with one of the leaders of the military or the political parties or any representative of the UN or other organisations that we called nongovernmental organisations, and of course and to keep a record of all the meetings. I was also making sure that the HQ was functioning properly with regards to the -- that is the secretaries, the security guards, the assistants, and I was also making sure that I was coordinating the agenda of the commander with the HQ and also with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. In the course of your duties, did you have a chance to see weapon sites, in particularly, artillery weapon sites, on either side of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. One, of course, had to be -- make sure to be able to have access to these sites particularly outside of Sarajevo, that is, in the Serb part. The access was particularly restricted and there was the exclusion zone of 20 kilometres that was put in place in February 1994. So from April 1993 until February 1994, what I was able to observe on the Serb side was quite restricted, however, on the main communication routes. And it was particularly in Lukavica and also the route between Lukavica and Pale, the road between Lukavica and Pale. As for after the exclusion zone was established, the 20-kilometre [Realtime transcript read in error "cent"] exclusion zone, obviously, after troops of the UN were deployed in different areas around Sarajevo, we were able to then be able to see the troops on the ground and to see the equipment and the weapons that were deployed around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not certain that the transcript mentions exactly what the witness said in relation to the number of the kilometres for the exclusion zone. Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 20-kilometre exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right. In February 1994, after the exclusion zone around Sarajevo was established, it was a 20-kilometre exclusion zone around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think what my friend was referring to was the second time he mentioned the exclusion zone, we have in the English transcript "cent," c-e-n-t. While you visited these weapon sites, artillery weapon sites, could you observe ammunition which was placed or brought there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. When we went on several occasions between Lukavica and Pale, in that road in particular, we went past very near some sites and we were able to see some artillery pieces, and we were also able to see some ammunition stockpiles which were near the pieces, near the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to the way these weapons positions were used, could you observe the way the Bosnian Serb forces would respond to Bosnian infantry attacks?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if there were operations or actions that came from the interior of Sarajevo that were attacking their troops along the line of the confrontation, then we didn't always know about such attacks, depending on where they were happening. But in several cases, we were able to -- when they were intense, we were able to know about them and the usual way was, and I believe that this was the case, the first response was with artillery fire or with mortar fire. It seems to me that the Serbs around Sarajevo didn't seem to have a lot of troops. So it was probably not of an infantry that were there able to able to riposte, to respond and to block, to counter attack. So, obviously, their superiority was to do with their artillery and their mortar pieces. So that was their way to stop any actions, operations, carried out by the Bosnian army along the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the Bosnian Serbs respond? Did they respond just on these infantry attacks, or were there other targets they engaged at those locations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: There were several reasons to start the artillery fire, as I mentioned earlier. The first reason was definitely a military reason, that is, there would be an operation against them, an action, and then they would counterattack, they would respond. If there was a Bosnian attack, then they would use their artillery, their mortars, their machine guns, any means to stop this attack. That would be the first reason. And then also there was also -- there were opportunity targets that could be presented, that is, for instance, if there were observers going around Sarajevo, if they could see either a military presence or a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. convoy or a target which had -- which was of major interest, of course, they would definitely be targeting, they would be firing at this target, again, using mortar and artillery. There were also artillery fire which didn't seem to be directed at any specific artillery target, and I believe this was a part of the strategy of a siege, that is, on those occasions, there would be firing at different locations inside the city of Sarajevo on targets, civilian targets, therefore, at times or in order to effect the morale of the inhabitants of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to distinguish what kind of civilian targets were engaged at those locations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand the question correctly, if there is a distinction. Were we able to tell whether this was a civilian or a military target? In some cases, both targets could overlap because Sarajevo is -- was a city under siege and, obviously, there were a lot of elements of a defence of Sarajevo which were located in civilian buildings. But also on several occasions, certainly on several occasions, there was firing that was targeted specifically at the civilian -- civilian population or civilian facilities in order to demoralise the population. They seemed to have no military operation interest. There was no military reason to do this. When we are talking about a queue of people waiting to get water, therefore, a water line, then we would be talking about civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. The shelling you had observed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, considering that there will have to be a cross-examination also done, I know this will be checked in the night, but I believe that Lieutenant-Colonel Bergeron said something else as well. Before the queue of people, he also mentioned a part from the water line, he mentioned something else as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which does not appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 25, Mr. President, second space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to influence the witness. If he said something else apart from the water line -- what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was people who were waiting also for the bread, either for water or for bread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The shelling you were able to observe in the time you were there which almost covered the year, was it at a continuous level or was there a time when it abated and perhaps later resumed? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. The shellings varied from one period to the other in intensity. Even during the course of one day, they could vary in intensity, depending on the time of day. There were periods when it was completely calm. There was a lull, and I believe I remember a period in 1993, for about a period of two months, there was a lull that lasted in the summer nearly two months, except that there was still sniper fire. This coincided with the high-level negotiations in Geneva and this was to do with very high instances of high-level negotiations between the factions. And this was manifested on the ground, if I can remember. I remember, for instance, that outside terraces were opening in Sarajevo again. There were a lot of repairs done to the utilities, that is, the water supply, the gas supply. There was a lot of work that was done during this period of time because of this lull in fighting. And I believe also that the tram inside the city of Sarajevo, for a part, started to work again. Therefore, we can see that it could go to zero, but then there were days that it went to more than 1.000 shells during one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why the -- if it resumed, and I guess it resumed because you said there was a lull of a couple of months. Do you know the reasons why the level of activity, to call it like that, resumed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: If we are talking about the longest lull in fighting while I was in Sarajevo, that is the summer of 1993, since I mentioned that this coincided with the high-level negotiations at that period of time. We were able to follow on the news that there were still some exchanges and this was to do with percentages of the territories for such-and-such a faction. And then when negotiations did not have a result, then obviously, shortly afterwards, the shelling resumed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at the time, or perhaps today, able to come to a conclusion as to the command and control the both warring factions had over their soldiers and officers in terms of the fact that it happened that there was a lull of such a long period during these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: In your question, you are asking me to comment on the two factions, on the two parties. Inside Sarajevo, during the year that I was there, I was able to see that there was a definite amelioration in terms of the organisation of the forces inside of Sarajevo, to the point that we were able to see new uniforms, new insignia, and everything else that was put in place in the course of the year. We could see that by the end of the fall, beginning of winter, 1993/1994, there were certain operations inside the actual troops of Sarajevo in order to take over the control inside of the city of the troops. And we can remember certain names, Celo and Caco, and these are people that were commanding the troops on the ground, but they were perhaps some elements that were criminal elements, gangsters. So the authorities, in each of the authorities inside themselves, inside their own forces, there was a kind of taking of control. There was, in fact, even an attack on these people in order to capture them, in order to take away the commandment from them and in order to put other people in their place. Definitely, there was an amelioration that was an improvement that was visible inside the city of Sarajevo. As for the Serb forces outside Sarajevo, throughout the time I was there, it was clear that General Galic, for me, in my opinion, was in effect commander of the Romanija Corps and he was in charge of everything that was going on around Sarajevo: all the negotiations, all the discussions, any talks that we had for the programme regarding the repair of the utilities, the facilities, the supplies, the gas, the electricity, and so on. We were always able -- we were always at the end of -- the bottom line was that we were always referred to speak to General Galic. If we had talks regarding the access to certain humanitarian convoys, again, the end of the line, it would always end up in General Galic's office. If we had any incidents to discuss, any protests, it was always to do with the office of General Galic. So, for me, it was very clear that General Galic, as the commander of the Romanija Corps, was in control of all the activities around Sarajevo. And if I can just come back to the famous period of February 1994, when there was -- the exclusion zone was established, the 20-kilometre exclusion zone, obviously, to start with, the negotiations were at a quite high level with Mr. Akashi, with the special representative, then with the commander of the UNPROFOR, then there was Mr. Izetbegovic who was involved, there was General Mladic who was involved. But when it came to actually finalise the details, the establishment of the area, the commander of the Sarajevo sector was designated as the one who was responsible on the ground. The Bosniaks had designated General Karavelic; and on the Serb side, it was General Galic who was named as continuing to put into place the exclusion zone in detail. And again, for me, this confirmed the status of General Galic, that he was the one who was in control and in command of what was going on around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, are you aware of an incident of the 31st of December, 1993, that involved tank fire?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of 1993, on that evening, the commander accompanied the Sarajevo sector commander outside. There was a special event. Barbara Hendriks was giving a recital. And whilst we were outside, the PTT building, which hosted the headquarters of the Sarajevo Sector, was hit not by an artillery shell but by a tank shell, and according to the trajectory, the arc, it was obvious that it was an indirect fire from a tank hitting or aiming at the headquarters as a welcoming card or just as reminder that there were people watching us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Can you please slow down a little bit because otherwise you are exhausting, on a Friday, the interpreters. Thank you very much. I would like the usher, please, to show to the witness Prosecution Exhibit P1367. Could you please, Lieutenant-Colonel, read on the first page, the title and the subject.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: [In English] Mortar attack at Dobrinja, June the 1st, at 10.20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also please indicate the title, the big letters you see just in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know which year this document refers to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you read out who the author of this crater analysis is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Captain Houdet, H-o-u-d-e-t, HQ company commander, Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how it comes about that you have seen this document and also explain to us what this document is all about.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. Following the -- let's call it the Dobrinja incident, mortar shells had fallen in a courtyard where children were playing. As a result, I can't remember how many people were killed but at least four had been killed, and this had been the cause of much talking in the Dobrinja neighbourhood, so much so that very quickly the Sarajevo Sector decided to send a team to do a crater analysis. We had Captain Houdet, who was a qualified analyst in our sector, so he went to the site to do all the measuring. He later came back to the headquarters and drafted this report. Upon his return to the headquarters, whilst he was finishing the report, I joined him in the operations room and I was able to see myself the results he had come to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. And what were those results?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: These results were later made public during the press conference in the Sarajevo Sector of the BH Command.
