Every morning, we would have a briefing, and following the crater analysis, during one of the following briefings, the results were made public. So once the analysis had been done, it was obvious that the fire had been coming from the Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss these findings with anybody from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Well, it was in a rather informal way. Some days later - I can't remember the exact date - not much later after the Dobrinja incident, the UNPROFOR commander was going to Lukavica. He was to meet with Mr. Karadzic, with General Mladic. I don't know what they were going to discuss. The Sarajevo commander and myself, we were in Lukavica during that meeting. At some point in time during the meeting, there was a break. People got out to do whatever they had to do, and then there came a time when Mr. Karadzic came closer to me, probably because he saw that I had a map in my hands, and on this map, this map of Sarajevo showing or so the confrontation line, I had myself marked the bearings which are here in this report by Captain Houdet. As I said earlier on, when I went to the operations room, I had realised that he was finishing his report, and I had made some handwritten markings to show the angles that he speaks about in his report. I did this because it was quite a major event and I figured we were bound to speak about it again some time later. Mr. Karadzic came closer to me, and quite in an informal way, asked me quite clearly so how we, the UN, we could be sure, certain, that the fire had most definitely been done from a Serb zone. I then showed him my map, the angles, and I very sort of succinctly explained to him how we had come to these findings: On the basis of the line of fire, the direction of fire, and by analysing the arc, we got to an area in which the mortar pieces were bound to have been sitting. And in the Dobrinja sector, this possible area where they could have been was entirely on the Serb side, and more specifically so, towards the south of Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any response from Mr. Karadzic or -- ?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: No. As I told you, this was, after all, a rather informal talk. He listened to me, to what I had to say. He looked at the map and thereafter he went, he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1994, early February 1994, was there a shelling at the Markale marketplace where you went to the scene?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, I was at what we called "the residence." It was the forward command post of the commander for Bosnia-Herzegovina, who at the time was General Rose. I had gone there alone with a driver. I was to coordinate some future activities with some members of his staff. And we were discussing various issues. People around us then told us that a very serious explosion had taken place on that marketplace you are speaking about. As I myself was not in the PTT headquarters, I decided to go there - I had to - but before I did so, and it was on my way, so I stopped at the marketplace. I got out of the vehicle. I just walked a little towards the area where the -- to the direction where the explosion had come from, apparently, and then later on I went back to the PTT building headquarters in Sarajevo, knowing that there was probably work to be done later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long, in your assessment, after the explosion happened, if you can tell us, did you arrive at the scene?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I must have been on the scene less than 10 minutes after the explosion, between 5 to 10 minutes, because the Residency or the res -- is very close to this place where the explosion took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you saw when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As I arrived, the situation was a very chaotic one. There were still some bodies lying dead on the ground. Other people were carrying some bodies away, and I saw one very close to me. He was taking the body of a man and he put that body into the boot of the area and the area rushed to the hospital -- the car rushed to the hospital. Sorry. A lot of shooting, of course, excited shouting. People were excited, upset. And as I said, I made a few steps towards the area where apparently the explosion seemed to have come from, and I saw tables or stalls that had been turned over, I saw bloodstains. But I did not go to the exact spot where the explosion took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there have you seen media people carrying television cameras?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I didn't notice that when I arrived, at least. I can't remember seeing either camera people or journalists. Although later on in the day, we saw news and footage that had been -- must have -- seemed to have been filmed straight after the explosion. So there must have been a few of them around, but I didn't notice them at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see people in uniform?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: There was a Canadian observer, Major Russel. He was at the Residency. We were not at the Residency for the same reasons, but he was there, too. And Major Russel was qualified to do crater analysis, so when the news came, he quickly went to the site. And I saw that this Major Russel was there, too, whilst I was on the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, if you could please spell the name of this Canadian UNMO.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: R-u-s-s-e-l, Major Russel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from this UNMO, were there any other people in uniform?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I did not notice that whilst I was there on the spot, but later on there was news or through talking to other people later on, I realised that there was another UNMO. I don't know his name. He was not a Canadian. So that was sure there was at least another UNMO there present on the site because we even saw him on the news. The crowd had sort of challenged him, wanted him to intervene, to do something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Waespi, may I just make a short announcement. Everything has been put in place to continue on at 2.00, so we have a bit more time. Before I send a final confirmation, I would just like to inform the parties. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go to a different subject, and this one will be the last but one. Are you aware of any hunting parties that operated within the Sarajevo theatre --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must adamantly oppose, object, to this wording, because it would imply from the Prosecution that there is an aim that something cruel, when you mean a "hunting party." This kind of wording is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can certainly rephrase and explain what is meant by an expression which was used by the witness in his witness statement, if you wish me to do so. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness used it in his witness statement, then -- nevertheless, I would prefer if you try to describe it in such a way as what you understand to mean those words, in more factual words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Russel -- I am sorry, Lieutenant Bergeron, are you aware of any people who came in from outside the Sarajevo war theatre to be engaged in sniping almost on a case-by-case basis and disappear again?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, so that we could understand the question properly, are we talking about fire that would come from inside Sarajevo towards the other side or the other way around, or both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please specify the question or -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be a question to the witness, whether he has seen different ways these snipers operated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The issue of the snipers was a very sensitive one throughout the year of my stay. On several occasions where we would meet with General Galic or people or members of his organisation, we would often mention the fact that there were snipers -- the fact that the snipers would kill civilians, be it women, children, elderly people, for apparently no other reason than to terrorise the population, than to demoralise the population. So, on several occasions, we would mention that this was very bad tactics on their part because the media, the international media, would always pick up on such events. There were photographs in the newspapers. The major media like CNN would take that up because that would happen in the very city, under the very eyes of the reporters who could very quickly move around and report on the events. So this was something that we found -- we found it difficult to understand. We didn't understand why they would carry on with such actions. And, of course, on the other hand, on the side of the Sarajevo people, whether they were Bosnians or Bosniaks or other nationalities within Sarajevo, during that year, it was often told to me that they were probably people coming from outside, not necessarily military people assigned to the Sarajevo siege but people who might have come from other parts of Bosnia or even outside Bosnia. We called them "weekenders." They would come from the weekend or for another day, and that is -- was told at the time that they were probably people who would come, say, for the weekend or for two days and who would occupy some of the sniper positions, Serb positions. And those people would shoot at civilians. Even among the UNPROFOR people, we would talk about this and we would try to get information from the observers. Indeed, we had observers on the Serb side, but their movements were rather restricted. But we never saw it ourselves without having any evidence of it as such. We thought that this was a very likely proposition, that people came from outside to occupy positions in order to use the situation to kill people. At the point in time it becomes difficult to make a difference between what you heard whilst you were there and what was reported later on because that was used by the media a lot. I can't remember in which magazine that was, but there was a whole story that was published where it was intimated that there were some kind of weekend warriors who would come to occupy the sniping positions for the weekend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn, and only briefly, to the last subject. How many times would you meet General Galic during your tenure in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Very often. Well, I didn't count the occasions, of course, but I would say at least 25 times. After all, there was -- we had developed some kind of a routine within the Sarajevo Sector with the various parties. And even when there was no major incident, we used to maintain some contact with the various parties. I don't know whether we can talk about an average, but not more than two weeks would go by without us meeting. And I say it again, if there was no major incident that had taken place, still, we would make an effort to have this type of meeting to maintain contact, to use the opportunity maybe to discuss other issues. So if you make a quick estimation, at least 25 times, yes, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the contents of those regular routine or perhaps not routine discussions you had with him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Of course, that could -- very depended on the incidents, on whether convoys had been stopped at a point. We would meet to take some steps so that the convoys would be allowed to go inside Sarajevo. It could be following incidents such as the Dobrinja incident or the marketplace incident that we mentioned. It could and it was, indeed, following incidents involving UNPROFOR staff, as you know. UNPROFOR personnel, including French, were killed on the airport area, on the Mount Igman area. So as soon, of course, if a man of ours would be killed, then we would try to meet with the parties to discuss that. But there was some kind of a routine, as much as we could, when we would meet the parties, and more specifically say if we talk about General Galic. When we would meet him, we were trying to stick to some kind of a procedure. And generally speaking, we would take stock of the situation, see what had happened since the previous meeting. In some cases we could mention, so if the time that had elapsed was one week we said, well, in the last seven days, we counted so many shelling, mortar shelling incidents, so many sniping, you know, "X" amount of casualties, as far as we knew. So we would report those figures recapitulating what had happened since the last meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this procedure, these meetings, and the way you described the way they happened, was that the procedure throughout that roughly year you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Obviously, this was not a very sort of strict or formal procedure. It was a habit that we had developed. And this modus operandi would apply more in meetings that had no particularly purpose, these meetings we had to maintain our contact. Of course, if there was a meeting following, say, the Dobrinja incident, of course, the discussion would revolve around Dobrinja and we would not mention three or four other topics. The idea then was to settle one specific incident or to deal with it in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question to clarify about the incident of the 31st of December 1993, which involved tank fire. Do you recall the position where the tank was stationed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Based on the sort of summary analysis that we did at the time, it was obvious that the shell came from a tank that was stationed around Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I will leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please leave the courtroom. [Interpretation] Now you will be cross-examined by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. In April 1993, when you were posted to the -- as the chef de cabinet of the Sector Commander, can you tell us how much did you know about the city of Sarajevo, how well were you informed about it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I can't say that I really knew very much when I left Canada, not specifically about the city of Sarajevo. Because as I have said already at the beginning of my testimony, I was first posted to Zagreb, to the UNPROFOR headquarters there. Therefore, I had general knowledge as to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, too. However, during the three weeks in Zagreb, realising that I would -- might be posted to Sarajevo, I began to show interest, to try to learn more about Bosnia and specifically about Sarajevo, so that I cannot say that I really had any substantive knowledge at the time when I arrived in Sarajevo. And it was the life in Sarajevo, because you have to remember that we were there 24 hours and we were in the city, we were talking with different factions. So to answer your question, no, I did not know much of Sarajevo at the time of my arrival, but in the months and weeks that followed, I believe I acquired, well, yes, I could say solid knowledge about what went on there in the city and around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you told us that you acquired solid knowledge for what went on there. Could you tell us, in the beginning of your testimony, you said that you were familiar with sites, with armaments sites, on the Serb side, as you said. Could you tell us when was it that you, for the first time, after you arrived you visited a site with the weapons stocks used by Bosnian Serbs in that part of the zone?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As I have already said, my stay in Sarajevo could be divided into two stages, different as regarding the possibilities to move around and observe weapons systems on the Serb side. Before the notorious exclusion zone, as I have already said, our movements were very restricted, especially before February 1994. What we could see of the weapons systems were those in Lukavica and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I ask you one thing. If you given an answer to a question and when the -- when counsel thinks that you touch upon areas which counsel thinks are less relevant, they are under a time restraint. So sometimes counsel would stop you and say, "Well, I would rather take you to another aspect of the question." If this would result in a situation where you would feel unhappy, since a specific aspect which is absolutely necessary for the understanding of what you said before, you may address the Chamber and ask whether you could continue. But otherwise, please accept the leading hand of counsel when they interrupt you. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, can you tell us when was it the first time that you visited weapons -- a weapons site on the Serb positions? Perhaps you do not remember that. If you do not, just please say so. If you do, then, please, again, tell us, when was that.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: No, I cannot give you an exact date. I can tell you that as of the first meeting that we had with the Romanija Corps, that is with General Galic or his representatives, as of that moment, we could go to Lukavica. And in Lukavica, around Lukavica, inside the barracks, there were certain weapon systems. And in the same vein, the first time that I went to Pale, on the way between Lukavica and Pale, we passed directly by certain positions where there were weapons stocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that you went by positions under the control of the Serb side and that you saw weapons on your way to Pale, that is, in that part between Lukavica and Pale, did you -- were you aware and had you been informed where the positions of the Bosniak army were? Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. Who was it that was supposed to inform me? Do you mean if anybody pointed out to me where their positions were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally, were you informed about the positions of the Bosniak army, of the BH army, at that time? Did you have any personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Just as much as the Serb positions are -- as I have said, when the UNPROFOR was deployed in Sarajevo specifically, we were under Chapter 5 so that our role was merely to escort humanitarian convoys. And in those cases --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR at the time did not have that kind of information, nor could we collect such information. We were -- we were seeing only what we could see and what the parties told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling us that those were the only positions of the belligerents, that is, the positions of the Serb army that you saw during your stay in Sarajevo? And it will be that part of the road that you told us you covered when you went to Pale and that you saw those weapon?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Until February 1994, those were, you could say, yes, the only weapons systems on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When we speak about weapons, about the armament, can you tell us how much did you know about the armament of the BH army, in the part of the city of Sarajevo controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Well, a little bit, obviously. Inside Sarajevo, we moved somewhat more freely, if not to all the places. Not everything was accessible to us. There is also the evident fact that we talked between ourselves, that is, the military and the military observers talked between themselves, and we had some idea about the types of weapons systems that existed inside the city. But I do not know exactly the positions that they were kept at. We didn't know exactly how they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, can you tell us whether you knew how many brigades there were in the 1st Corps, which was in the part of Sarajevo under the BH army's control?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As I told you, when I was not doing any intelligence, military intelligence gathering, we talk about the commander level because at the brigade it was the battalions inside Sarajevo that maintained coordination with the brigades. We were at the level of the commander, for instance, towards the end, with General Karavelic. But we know, as is true of all military operations, it was sort of divided. So within a corps, there are brigades within the corps, maybe three, four, five or six, I don't know. But I don't have an exact figure. I said this earlier on, I know that during the year, there was a reorganising of the Sarajevo forces. Did that increase or reduce the number of brigades? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, if I tell you that there is a document made up by UNMOs during the period of time relevant to Sarajevo, that is between 1993 and 1994, and that was in 1993 that there were 10 brigades, would that piece of information be acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Well, this figure of 10, I can't confirm it. And I was about to say that the forces inside Sarajevo improved throughout the year of my stay. There were visible signs thereof, of this improvement in command and control, but also in the way that army was organised. It was equally obvious that they had much more infantry available inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. So you are telling us that you were not informed, that you had no knowledge of the command post of the brigades and battalions in these brigades and smaller units. You are telling us that you had no knowledge where they were, what facilities were they stationed in?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Once again, refer back to my position: I was chief of cabinet. I was not specialised in intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to apologise for not knowing something. Ms. Pilipovic is just asking you whether you know it or not. And if you don't know it, just tell us that you don't know it. I mean, as I told you before, the Defence is under some time restraint. So, therefore, just start to give the information specifically asked for and if the Defence would like to have further information from you, I am certain that they will put further questions in that respect to you. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about the -- you have told us about the reorganisation of the 1st Corps in a part of the city of Sarajevo under the control of the 1st Corps, and you also said that at times accounts were squared between individual formations. Could you tell us what shape did these settling of scores take? How were they settling the accounts between them? And I mean units within the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: We learned that, among other things, through these visible signs: There was firing, there were attacks within the city. So we soon realised that these were Bosnians attacks other Bosnians in some way. And as I said, we had battalions with liaison officers, we had observers on the ground, and then even the Bosnian military confirmed this to us without giving us too many details, but they confirmed that they had pulled out of their command certain individuals. So that they'd sort of tidied up within their ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you tell us that you had information about fire, about shots being fired, do you have any knowledge as to the outcome of that, whether there were any casualties in those parts where this fighting was taking place, that is, do you have any more specific knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As far as I know, these were not operations of a very large extent. It was rather focused onto one specific building where some people might have sought refuge. Like Caco and Celo, I couldn't tell you how many people were killed among their men. I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any civilians were victimised during those settlings of accounts?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak about the reorganisation and operation of some units within the 1st Corps of the BH army, did you know during your term of duty there that there was a battalion which controlled the Butmir area? I mean the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of the confrontation lines, and when you go down from Mount Igman, you would come into the Butmir village. But personally, I never went inside Butmir. There was probably a commander commanding Butmir, but I have no information on this. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information that those troops that were in Butmir - and you will agree with me that Butmir was controlled by the Bosnian army - that fire was opened from that area, targeting the airport area, mortar fire I mean, and that during the period of time when you were in Sarajevo, that there were casualties amongst French troops?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier on, we mentioned the Dobrinja case, which was a very clear-cut one. But throughout the year, in most cases, we were not able to confirm with any degree of certainty that a round might have come or could have only come from the Serb zone. In most cases when we would carry out this type of analysis, we arrived at a possibility that the shell could have come either from the Bosnian or from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in view of your function during your tour of duty, how much and were you informed about the activity of snipers in the territory of the city of Sarajevo, that is, in the territory of the city controlled by the BH army and the part of the city controlled by the army of Republika Srpska? Were you personally informed about this, and how?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I am sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt my learned colleague but the question she had asked before was a multiple question, and the witness answered just by "yes." So it is a little bit difficult to figure out what -- to which parts, if anything, he said. It's the question which had started with, and I quote: "Did you have any information that those troops that were in Butmir... " And so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will rephrase my question. I will make it more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, during your tour of duty in Sarajevo, did you have any knowledge, any information, about the operations conducted by the Bosnian troops from Butmir targeting the airport?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As I said, I can't remember a specific incident where we could say with as much certainty as for the Dobrinja incident. I can't remember any one where we can say with 100 per cent certainty that that fire came from Butmir. I mean, the analysis are not that specific, could have come from Butmir, but it could have come from next door just from the Serb-controlled part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if, during your duty there, any analysis was carried out specifically in the airport area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I know that there were, after all, several French people who were killed on the airport, and measurements and analysis were carried out, but I can't remember the exact findings because this was done by the French Battalion that was there stationed on the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I asked you whether you personally, and how, were informed about snipers under the BH army's control and VRS's control?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Personally, I never saw a sniper shooting. I was informed through daily reports from the observers or from the battalions deployed inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you received reports, can you tell us whether -- what did these reports say about sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Well, these were -- we are not talking here about the analysis reports. We are talking about daily reports on the type of activities that had taken place in and around Sarajevo, depending on the means that the UNPROFOR had. And the means were basically the observers. In their reports, the number of rounds was recorded, the number of snipers was recorded. Of course, we knew it did not represent everything that had happened but only accounted for what had been observed. It was mentioned whether there had been fire from either side and the number of casualties as had been observed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you received such reports, can you tell us if your personnel, that is, UNPROFOR and UNMOs, would they go out to the scenes of sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I would say that we did not go in all cases, that is for sure. In some cases -- I will remind you that there was a division of the city in zones, according to responsibility. Each battalion deployed had a zone of responsibility. So it is a combination of UNMOs' observations and of the battalions as deployed within Sarajevo. They were able to go on to the scenes to see the facts that had been reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, do you know how many investigations were conducted following sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I couldn't give you any figure. I couldn't tell you how many incidents, how many investigations there were. But, of course --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that you received reports, can you also tell us about these reports? You tell us that they were UNMO reports. Can you tell us, who were they submitted to when it comes to the warring parties in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: No. Well, the type of reports I am speaking about are UNPROFOR reports that we had to prepare every day, and they were transmitted to the higher command. The Sarajevo Sector would transmit a report on the last -- on the previous 24 hours to the BH Command in Kiseljak. As to the UNMO's reports, they were sent directly to Zagreb, to the observers' chief, and he was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, when you spoke about shelling, you said that there was a period -- that in 1993 there was a period of total calm in Sarajevo. Then you also said that there were periods when 1.000 shells would fall in a day. I believe that is what you said. So can you tell us what areas were under the heaviest shell fire during your tour of duty on both sides?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Most definitely, they are the zones along the confrontation line, among other places, towards the south-east of the said zone, and a lot also in the north, north-west area of the zone. But there again, this is my better understanding of the situation. But a fair deal was along the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Bergeron, when you spoke about south-east, did you have any personal knowledge as to the military units present in the area and which side those units belonged to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. We know that there were many operations, Bosnian operations that is, towards the confrontation line in order to try and cut off the route or the road from Pale to Lukavica, and especially so in the Brajkovac area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how frequent were those operations and what was the incidents of such offensives that you tell us were launched by the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: There must have been some that we didn't know of, depending on how big they were. But for the one around Brajkovac, where apparently the objective was to capture strategic points around Brajkovac, during my stay, I was made aware of at least two major operations in that sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I am looking at the clock and wonder whether, would this be a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn until 2.00 this afternoon. I would like to see you back -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might you clarify what time we might finish today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have -- we have available to ourselves the services of the interpretation that would be available to the Stakic case this afternoon. But I think one hour and-a-half has been -- so 3.30 would be the time. But that is what I expect, as a matter of fact, might be five minutes later or sooner. It also depends a bit on how things develop this afternoon. General Galic, you will have a longer pause now for one hour and a half. I am not fully aware, although you informed us before, about, well, the way you could rest during the -- during the break. If there is any reason upon resuming at 2.00 that you feel not fit to follow the proceedings or if at any later moment you would feel that you would lose concentration to such an extent that it would be inappropriate to proceed, would you please inform me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will do so in time. But I believe I will manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we will adjourn until 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, once the witness has been brought into the courtroom, you may resume the cross-examination. And I take that you have 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, today during the examination-in-chief you were shown a document 1367 in relation to the crater analysis of the 1st of June, 1993. Could you tell us when did you receive the information about the incident that took place on the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the very same day, in the hours that followed the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when the crater analysis was done, was carried out?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: It was in the days that followed the incident. It was either the following day or it was two days later, which was more or less one or two days later, maximum two days after the incident had taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you received the information the incident had taken place, could you tell us who was it that you received the information from?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I did not personally receive the information. The information was received at the HQ of Sarajevo through the operations room, and after that, the word spread that there had been an incident that had taken place in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally go to see the place where the incident had happened?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: No, I did not go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you tell us that the analysis was carried out either one day later or two days later, could you tell us, when was it that you saw officially the document on the crater analysis that was done?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I saw Captain Houdet when he returned from his reconnaissance or, rather, his analysis of the ground, after he took some data, when he returned to the HQ. What I don't remember, whether it was the next day or two days later. But I assume it could not have been much later. It could not have been more than one day after the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what other information, what other pieces of information did you have after this incident of the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: We knew that there was a certain number of dead, among them, children. And as I mentioned this morning, I do not remember the exact number. It is probably in one of the reports that we submitted following this incident. But as far as I can recall, it would be at least four people who died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, did you have any information that a number of soldiers were also killed during this incident?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that a report was compiled following this incident, could you tell us who was this -- to whom was this report forwarded to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Again, as I mentioned this morning, every day there was a report of facts on the activities that had taken place in the last 24 hours. So as soon as the report of the Sector Sarajevo would be completed, they would also contain information relating to this incident. And then, equally, regarding the incident that had taken place in Dobrinja, there was a letter of protest that was drafted by the HQ of the Sector Sarajevo and that was transmitted or was forwarded to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that a letter of protest was drafted and it was send to the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, could you tell us when was this letter delivered and who received it at the command?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I did not send this letter. We had a section, we had a department in the HQ whose responsibility it was to draft letters of protest. And for your information, there were letters of protest nearly every day, not necessary to the Serb authorities, but it was also to the Bosnian authorities, depending on the activities and the incidents that took place. But there was a standard procedure that letters of protest, at the latest, would be drafted 24 hours following an incident, normally speaking, and then they would be transmitted, normally speaking, to the liaison officer of different party who were -- who were residing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bergeron. Could you confirm, personally, you, do you know whether such a letter was sent to the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps or according to the work of the UNPROFOR and the way that the reports were compiled, you presume that this was done within everyday procedure?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: In fact, I think I remember or, rather, I am presuming that this letter was sent to the superior level. Depending on the nature of the incidents, it happened that the letter of protest was sent to a superior network. It could have been directly sent to General Mladic. So depending on the nature of the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Bergeron, you don't know whether this was either sent to the Main Staff or the HQ or to the command, you are just assuming that it was sent?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bergeron, you said that you had 25 meetings, approximately, with General Galic. One of the topics at these meetings was also humanitarian aid. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your mandate, could you confirm to us that there were abuses of humanitarian convoys in order to transport weapons to parts of the city that were under the control of the BH army, in order to arm the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: If you are asking me if I knew that humanitarian convoys were transporting weapons, my answer is no, I never knew about such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to remind you, during your mandate - and that was on the 9th of April, 1993 - do you have any knowledge, and I can refresh your memory, that a humanitarian -- that a convoy was stopped in the area of Ilidza and it was established that that convoy contained ammunition of Arabic manufacture, origin, and other weapons and armaments? That was on the 9th of April 1994. Did you have any information in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I do not recall this incident. It was by the end of my tour of duty. I am not certain, but it doesn't -- it doesn't ring a bell, this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the incident that happened on the 1st of June in Dobrinja. Do you have any knowledge whether in relation to this incident, other authorised bodies carried out crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no other analysis effect apart from the analysis done by Captain Houdet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, during your tenure can you confirm to us that there was an agreement that was concluded about the withdrawal of forces from Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica, the withdrawal of forces of the Republika Srpska army? Do you have any knowledge that such an agreement had been signed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that there was an agreement on Mount Igman so that the Serb forces withdraw from Mount Igman and that the UNPROFOR forces can be inserted in their place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether UNPROFOR forces respected this agreement on the withdrawal from Igman and Bjelasnica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we deployed Sarajevo troops on Mount Igman and we then -- we had permission to deploy French forces and then Ukrainian. We occupied the ground as it was restricted and as it was agreed on by different parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that the BH army violated this agreement and that it carried operations out in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I remember that I had seen and I had read, there were always reports that we read on a daily basis. Yes, there were incidents that were reported on Mount Igman. You have to know that this is a mountainous area. It is a mountain and also wooded, and there were a lot of movement of troops in that mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, at that time did you receive information that the army of BH from Mount Igman was shelling the area of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly about the shellings from Mount Igman towards Ilidza. I remember of operations that had been carried out from Igman, but not of this one in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you remember about the operations that were carried out from Mount Igman, could you tell us which operations were there and at what time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: This is my answer: What I mean is that I don't remember specific operations with a specific date. But I remember that there were -- in reports, it was mentioned that there was movement of troops, that there was certain incidents that occurred on Mount Igman and involving BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, during your tenure, could you confirm to us that the agreement on collection of heavy weapons of Sarajevo was also signed on the 19th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: That is correct. If we are talking about the agreement linked to the exclusion zone, the 20-kilometre exclusion zone, that is right, there was this agreement that was signed, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm to us or, rather, could you agree with me that on the Serb side or from the Serb side, this agreement was respected while you were at your post?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking. As a matter of fact, the agreement -- of course, it was some time before it had entered into force. But all of the weapons with prohibited calibres were withdrawn for 20 kilometres, and those that could not have been withdrawn, then there was the UNPROFOR presence placed there near and in the vicinity of these weapons that could not be moved. So, yes, they respected the agreement during my tenure, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the concentration of weapons during the collection of heavy weapons? What was the concentration of weapons on the side of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As far as I recall, we had collected not very many weapons on the inside -- inside of Sarajevo. The weapons were all massed in one place, in the Tito Barracks as we called it. And there were some mortars. That is more or less everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that the Defence has information that BH army had tanks at the time and that there were three to five tanks at the time, could you confirm that this information is correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I have never seen tanks, apart from destroyed tanks, inside Sarajevo. So if there were tanks, they were well camouflaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that there were cannons, Howitzers?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were only mortars inside of Sarajevo. But, again, our movements were quite restricted inside the city in a certain way. But anything is possible. However, personally, I was never informed that there were cannons, for instance, 105 millimetres, 155 millimetres, inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, when you are talking about mortars, do you have any information about the activity of mobile targets, for instance, use of vehicles on which mortars were mounted and that the BH army used in such a way so that from some parts of the city they would fire these mortars? Specifically, do you have any information that such mobile targets were used in the vicinity of the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I know that on several occasions there were reports or, rather, there were complaints from the Bosniak side that there were -- that there were certain mobile targets that were moving near certain buildings, near some civilian buildings, that there were firing. I am not -- don't remember specifically the PTT building was involved. But, yes, as a matter of fact, they were -- like all the forces, they had mobile equipment. And it was known that Bosniak authorities may have authorised their placement near civilian buildings and may have authorised them firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask for a clarification. The transcript says that there were complaints from the Bosnian side. Should that be the Serbian side or from the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What want to say is that we, the UNPROFOR side, we were writing letters of protest and we were presenting them to the Bosnian side because they were firing mortars near civilian buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would be complaining to the Bosnian side. It now reads "from," complaints from the Bosnian side. But perhaps that is a matter of language. The UN was complaining to the Bosnians about what they did? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was a violation as far as we were concerned. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I used your last minute, but, --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, with your leave --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bergeron, during your mandate, did you receive any information that in the area of the city of Sarajevo under the control of the BH army, that there were camps or prisons? Did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: No. This is not something that I knew anything about, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that there were prisons called Stela, Silos, Tarcin, where Serbs were imprisoned? Did you have any such information? Did you receive any such information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: It is not a kind of information I remember, no. I don't remember, no. I am not saying that it didn't exist, but I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. Bergeron. How much were you informed about the activities of snipers of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Again, I don't have very good knowledge of specific activities on such a date. But according to the reports that we received and what was observed on the ground, we knew that there were also obviously snipers who were operating on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Waespi, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you mentioned that there were snipers who were able to go -- come into the city and leave the city. How could -- how would they be able to do it if the population in general was not -- they were not able to do that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't quoted well because what I said was that, from the Serb positions, there were snipers who were able to come from the outside of the city, who were able to come from the outside of Sarajevo from other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina or even from outside of Bosnia, in order to join certain Serb positions who were overhanging Sarajevo or around Sarajevo. This was around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes, now I understand. Another question: According to the testimonies that we have heard here, the firing of tanks, where there was direct fire, but you spoke here referring on the firing on the PTT building, you spoke about indirect fire. How could you explain this contradiction, this apparent contradiction?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: This is a little bit of a military jargon but when we are talking about tanks, yes, most of the tanks would go for the direct hit. That means that they would see the target on which they want to fire and they would be firing directly on that target. It would be like somebody firing with a rifle, with a gun. On the other hand, since we look at the inclination of the tank, if we know the position, then it becomes like an artillery piece, not quite, but if we -- if people are firing at an angle and without knowing exactly where the target is -- without knowing exactly where the target is, then we know roughly where the firing we get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You see the target?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: No, you don't see the target. It will be the oblique trajectory that would then -- that is why we would call it indirect fire. Without seeing the target, it would then be in an arch. Then this is a way of getting to the target, not in a very precise way, but still it would get to the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge El Mahdi has a question for you. [In English] I must apologise, I have forgotten to put my microphone on when I said, [Interpretation] Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions to you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I understood that you said that the damage, that the worst damage, the most serious damage was done along the confrontation line. In your opinion, is there a parallel between a confrontation line and military targets? My question, I am going to have to explain it. Could we conclude from this, from what you said, that in essence military targets, "confrontation line," quote, unquote, and those small areas, were those that were most targeted, or were they essentially the targets of fire?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I am just going to be a little -- add a little clarification and a specification. You said that I had said that the most important damage -- the most considerable damage was along the confrontation line. What I really said was that the most of the shelling -- I don't know the damage that was a result of that but we are talking about the shelling this morning. So what I said is that the majority of the shelling took place or the impacts arrived around the confrontation line, in the areas around the confrontation line, where the combatants were, the troops, facing each other were. So it is in that sense, and, yes, as a matter of fact, what I believe happened was that all of the shelling that happened inside the Sarajevo, most of them - I cannot tell you exactly a percentage - but I believe that the vast majority was directed as the examples that I gave this morning, to stop a Bosnian attack, for instance, the troops that were moving or an attack, an assault, in order to stop the targets of opportunity. Most of those attacks happened around the confrontation line. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. We can, however, conclude at least not to rule out the hypothesis that the shelling outside of this area was intentional, was deliberate? Or was it not deliberate, unintentional, since there was this explanation in order to fix the angle of the firing, it still needed a certain military manoeuvre and a certain amount of work done. So you could, however, say that the shelling outside of this area or near this area was in some way, the damage, that it was inevitable in some way?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: "Collateral," in military jargon. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, in order not to say "collateral." Do you rule out this possibility?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I would, however, like to qualify it because, yes, as a matter of fact, when we are talking about pieces that were moving, cannons, if we moved the cannons and here we have the main battery, if, as a matter of fact, there is a period of adjustment of several shells, that what is needed is the expertise of the marksman. However, yes, there were -- pieces were not also static. But there were also pieces that were static, weapons that were static and for some time. So the coordinates, the angles, all the charges necessary was certainly recorded. I assume that from starting points, Serb army already had maps of firing with targets recorded, with elevations, all the necessary facts in order to adjust their firing because they had already targeted and fired at these locations for quite a long period of time. So it is a "yes and no" answer: "yes" for the mobile pieces, but it is "no" in some other cases when the pieces or the weapons were already in those places for some period of time. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Just a slight clarification, please. This is in relation to what you said. During the effort of the army, or rather the command of the army, of the Presidency army, to have an effective command and control on some of their factions inside their troops, you spoke of some exchange of fire which took place between units of the army of the Presidency and some groups, and that this had caused some civilian victims. How long did it last, this operation? Was this a one-day or two-day operation or did this go on for months?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Well, from what we knew about it or, rather, the most important, the most famous that we could see the effects on the ground itself, this operation must have lasted about 48, 72 hours. This operation took away Celo and Caco. As far as I remember, this was an operation, 72 hours. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] However, this operation did cause some civilian deaths?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: There were losses, I know, but I don't know how many. I don't know the details. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions for you as well, Mr. Bergeron. The first is: You told us this morning that sniping was mentioned in meetings with General Galic and that you found it difficult to understand that they continued sniping. And then a few lines further, you said: "It was often told to me that there were probably people coming from outside." And then you told us about, well, the weekend warriors, if I may call it. It was often told to you by whom? Because it is part of an answer that deals in one respect with General Galic, meetings with General Galic, and it is not clear to me what was the source, who told you about these weekend warriors.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Again, I would just like to be a little bit accurate. When we are talking about sniper activity inside the city, as a matter of fact, there were. There were dead. We saw them. We counted them in certain situations and so on. Now the point to know whether there were people from outside the city, as I mentioned this morning, and this is something I cannot certify; I cannot confirm for sure, but obviously the Bosniaks on the inside told us these things and we in the UNPROFOR, we spoke to each other. We spoke about it. We spoke to the UNMOs, the observers. And at the end of the day, we came to the conclusion that this was a possibility. This is all I can say. I cannot say this is a certainty. But the more we talked about it, the more we looked, the more we observed, the more we believed that this was a possibility that this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This information had nothing to do with your meetings with General Galic but came from elsewhere, from -- not within the city.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question. We -- you have testified this morning about the crater analysis by Captain Houdet. May I first ask you one question: If I read in this crater analysis "angle of descent," should I consider an angle of descent to be the angle between the -- well, the direction in which the shell falls and the horizon?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: As I said, I am not a specialist in crater analysis. But if I understand correctly, this is -- the angle of descent is in relation to the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did read the crater analysis, you confronted, in an informal way, Mr. Karadzic with the results. May I take it that you have read it and that you would agree with the conclusions of Mr. Houdet?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the fact that he was qualified. He had the expertise to interpret this and to have the analysis of the facts, of the data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... try or may I ask you to try and follow me in how I understand the findings of Mr. Houdet and then see whether we all come to the same conclusions. Madam Registrar, could you please, with the assistance of the usher, give a sketch number one to the witness and to the parties and the accused and, of course, to the other Judges. Could you please, Mr. Usher, put it on the ELMO. Yes. What I tried to do is to visualise what I think I read in the crater analysis. I indicated with letter "A" the angle of descent that would be allowed by the surrounding buildings. And I did put a letter "B" where we talk about the minimum angle of descent for 81 millimetre and 120 millimetre mortars. Does my understanding of what the crater analysis say correspond with your understanding?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing which should be done is that one should continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Just for the first part. Then, Madam Registrar could you please give a document number two. On number two, I try to visualise in addition to the other sketch an angle of descent of, let's say, approximately 70 degrees. Would that, keeping in mind what would be the minimum angle of descent, would that be a possible angle of descent? I mean, is my understanding of what a "minimal angle of descent is," would that correspond with a possible angle of descent as indicated under "C"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: If I rely on Mr. Houdet's notes, that would not be possible. This would not be possible, if I rely on the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that the minimum angle of descent in your understanding would be that it is either a more flat trajectory and it could not be a higher trajectory? Would that mean that the --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: No. I think that I have to come back -- I have to change my answer, in fact. I should -- I should agree with your interpretation, yes. As a matter of fact, yes, because it could have gone this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please have a look at a third sketch I prepared. I tried to visualise here what approximately might be the consequence of a more flat or a more steep angle of descent. According to this sketch, the minimum range of fire for line "B" would not allow any conclusion -- would not allow the conclusion that it should have been fired at a distance not closer than the firing point of trajectory "B." I am just wondering, what I tried to do is understand what line of reasoning was in the report of Captain Houdet, and I had some difficulties in understanding. Therefore, I tried to interpret how I - and I am not the only one in the Chamber - how I would understand what he established and what consequences that might have. And I am asking you, since you -- I am more or less asking you now to choose between the conclusions of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Captain Houdet and the attempt of this Chamber to understand the findings of Captain Houdet.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: It is certain that it would be better to have Captain Houdet here. I am sure you are aware of that. And here I wouldn't want to testify as a ballistics expert or a crater analysis expert, because I am not that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having followed this provisional line of thought, whether you would still stick to the conclusions of Captain Houdet, or that you would leave it open, or that you would have some comment on our attempt to understand the situation.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I understand very well what you are trying to understand, but if I can say that in the heat of the moment, what really it was the angle that caught my attention, and then the interpretation, to look at the designated zone, which said that the mortar had to be in one of this area, anywhere in that particular box. And the whole box was within the Serb territory. That was what happened. But I didn't have all the other interpretation and all the curves and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know where the woods are, but if you find the wood between 1120 metres from the point of impact or 1340 metres from the point of impact, a bit further on, that you might locate the mortars in that wood because of the consequences you have drawn out of the data you have collected. I am just trying to understand. There are data in this crater analysis, and there are conclusions, and I am trying to understand how these conclusions are a logical outcome of the data that has been taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: I have to repeat, I am not a technical expert to explain the angles, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi. I am not entirely ready, so if you have any additional questions in this respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, just a hint, perhaps. As you know, we have a mortar expert coming and perhaps this person, since Lieutenant-Colonel Bergeron said he was not an expert in that, he could have a closer look at your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we should ask perhaps a mortar expert to come as well. But I don't know whether the Prosecution is going to -- I mean, it is through this witness that the crater analysis was presented. And this witness, well, at least gave a firm impression that he would understand and follow the conclusions of Captain Houdet. So this does not exclude any further examination of other experts or witnesses on this subject. Just one moment. Yes. You told us before that you had a map in your hands when you saw Mr. Karadzic. And you also said, "And on this map, this map of Sarajevo, showing also the confrontation line, I had myself marked the bearings which are here in this report of Captain Houdet." Could you tell us exactly what you are talking about, if you said that you marked the bearings that are in the report of -- whether those confrontation lines or point of impact or what was that? Or was it one of the maps attached to the crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: That is right. It's the second map, which shows the point of impact in Dobrinja, and from the point of impact, there are two lines that go towards south-east. On this very same map, there is a minimum range that we spoke about. So according to this, it means that this mortar, the box, is basically -- that he spoke about, goes from the edge of the minimum range, and then he goes further. So the mortars could have been anywhere in between within this perimeter. And according to what Captain Houdet said, it could not be any more further up in the X. It couldn't be anywhere further -- it could not have been anywhere nearer Dobrinja than it was already marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... basis of his report, which the Chamber tried to understand.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN BERGERON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers. Since the Chamber did put a lot of questions, are there any additional questions in this specific respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we have a short break? Because one of our colleagues is coming down. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is not -- I thought you would be prepared, but -- I mean, it is a Prosecution exhibit that we discussed. So this would at least conclude, for this moment, the examination of this witness, but if we would have a break now, we intended to continue until 3.30. I don't know how much time you would need and whether it would be possible perhaps to continue with another witness and perhaps ask Mr. Bergeron not yet -- not to leave the building yet and see whether there is any need to recall him on today, if the Chamber would allow such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it would be preferred if we could start with the next witness, and perhaps at the end of the day, if there is any need for re-examination, do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we have to keep in mind whether all the supporting interpreters and staff is still available then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may assist, we are a little bit handicapped because as is often the case, unfortunately, the LiveNote has stopped working on our machine, which handicaps us from going back to earlier text. If we switch now to Mr. Philipps, I think we need a short break in any event to set up the PowerPoint. Perhaps during that break someone could attend to the LiveNote and perhaps we could recall Mr. Bergeron at, say, 20 past 3.00 or 25 past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is there need for the other technical support also?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. For Mr. Philipps, we will need a short break to set up the PowerPoint.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no break required. The technician can come in and do it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. In that case, then -- all right, yes. Perhaps the LiveNote technician could come in now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They have been called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, anyhow, for five minutes, and during the break, the Chamber will decide on whether an opportunity will be given, if the Prosecution would ask to do so, to put further questions to Mr. Bergeron. The Chamber notes already that the issue of the report, and the conclusions to be drawn out of that report, were both in chief and in cross dealt with, so there is nothing specifically new about the questions the Chamber has put. Mr. Bergeron, may I -- may I ask you to remain available for the next -- during this afternoon? It might be that you will not be recalled. That would mean that this would have then concluded your testimony in this court. And if you are not recalled, I already thank you for having come and having answered all the questions of the parties and of the Chamber. But perhaps we will see each other back later this afternoon. We will adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would just like to inform the Chamber that today in the courtroom we have the expert of Defence, Lieutenant General Dr. Radovan Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome into this courtroom. Before we continue, Mr. Ierace, the Chamber has considered -- we do not oppose against additional questions, but I don't know whether it could be done right away, or that you -- if you say you need more time to consult experts --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I don't seek to ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. That means that there will be no recall of -- yes. Okay. Then could you please call your -- yes, we first have to -- yes. I always know quite well how to deal with documents, but I think marking for identification my own sketches will preserve them for history.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1367, crater analysis; Exhibit P1367.1, B/C/S translation; document marked for identification number 13, diagram; marked for identification number 14, diagram; marked for identification number 15, diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibits are admitted into evidence and the other documents are marked for identification. Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I call Richard Philipps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, I take it that you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Philipps. Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Richard Philipps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you born in 1962?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a military analyst in the military analysis team of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your education, did you receive a Bachelor of Arts? And if so, from which institutions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I received a Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of London, in French and linguistics, and also from the University of Grenoble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, are you a British citizen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some stage, did you join the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I was commissioned into the territorial army in 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What training have you undergone in the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I was an officer cadet from 1981 to 1994, part-time. And then after being commissioned in 1985, I underwent training in the intelligence corps in the British Army part-time as an analyst. Further to that, I have attended various courses at military colleges, including the Staff College.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remain a member of the territorial army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
utterances.text: I am still an officer in the territorial army in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now by way of employment, have you any employment background in analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS
